DISCLAIMER OF INHERITANCE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Pat Morgan

WHO MAY DISCLAIM, AND THE BASIC RIGHT TO DISCLAIM
Under California Probate Code § 262, a “beneficiary” is the person entitled, but for a disclaimer, to take an interest — the person who would otherwise receive property, whether from Pat Morgan's estate or some other source covered by this part. Section 264 uses a separate term, “disclaimant,” for whoever actually executes the disclaimer: that can be the beneficiary personally, or someone else acting on the beneficiary's behalf, such as a guardian, conservator, or personal representative acting for a minor, a conservatee, or a deceased beneficiary (Prob. Code §§ 276–277 separately require a court order before that kind of representative's disclaimer on another person's behalf becomes effective). Section 275 then states the core right in a single sentence: a beneficiary may disclaim any interest, in whole or in part, by filing a disclaimer as provided in this part.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Beneficiary” means the person entitled, but for the person’s disclaimer, to take an interest."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 262, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — definition of “beneficiary” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=262.)
  "“Disclaimant” means a beneficiary who executes a disclaimer on his or her own behalf or a person who executes a disclaimer on behalf of a beneficiary."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 264, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — definition of “disclaimant” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=264.)
  "A beneficiary may disclaim any interest, in whole or in part, by filing a disclaimer as provided in this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 275, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — the core right to disclaim, in whole or in part (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=275.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes three separate sections of California Probate Code Division 2, Part 8 — §§ 262, 264, and 275 — each independently fetched twice (two separate requests using distinct User-Agent strings against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) with identical results both times; they are three distinct sections of the same statutory part, not three unrelated sources. The parenthetical reference to the guardian/conservator/personal-representative court-order requirement in Prob. Code §§ 276–277 is drawn from the same verified fetch of those two sections but is not independently quoted in this clause; a reader concerned with disclaiming on behalf of a minor, conservatee, or decedent should consult those sections' full text directly.

WHAT COUNTS AS A DISCLAIMABLE “INTEREST”
California Probate Code § 267 defines “interest” broadly for purposes of the disclaimer statute. Subdivision (a) covers the whole of any property, real or personal, legal or equitable, any fractional part or share of it, any estate in it, any power to appoint, consume, apply, or expend property, and any other right, power, privilege, or immunity relating to property. Subdivision (b) then lists fifteen specific ways an interest can be created that fall within this definition, and states that the list is illustrative rather than exhaustive (“includes, but is not limited to”). The listed categories reach well beyond a probate-estate inheritance: they include an interest created by intestate succession or under a will, but also an interest under a trust, an interest created by succession to a previously disclaimed interest, an interest arising from an election to take against a will, a power of appointment (whether its creation, or its exercise or nonexercise), an inter vivos gift outright or in trust, an interest arising from surviving the death of a depositor of a Totten trust account or P.O.D. account, an interest under an insurance or annuity contract, an interest arising from surviving the death of another joint tenant, an interest under an employee benefit plan, an interest under an individual retirement account, annuity, or bond, an interest under a transfer-on-death beneficiary designation in a deed or other instrument, and a final catch-all for “any other interest created by a testamentary or inter vivos instrument or by operation of law.”

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) “Interest” includes the whole of any property, real or personal, legal or equitable, or any fractional part, share, or particular portion or specific assets thereof, or any estate in any such property, or any power to appoint, consume, apply, or expend property, or any other right, power, privilege, or immunity relating to property. (b) “Interest” includes, but is not limited to, an interest created in any of the following manners: (1) By intestate succession. (2) Under a will. (3) Under a trust. (4) By succession to a disclaimed interest. (5) By virtue of an election to take against a will. (6) By creation of a power of appointment. (7) By exercise or nonexercise of a power of appointment. (8) By an inter vivos gift, whether outright or in trust. (9) By surviving the death of a depositor of a Totten trust account or P.O.D. account. (10) Under an insurance or annuity contract. (11) By surviving the death of another joint tenant. (12) Under an employee benefit plan. (13) Under an individual retirement account, annuity, or bond. (14) Under a transfer on death beneficiary designation in a deed or other instrument. (15) Any other interest created by a testamentary or inter vivos instrument or by operation of law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 267, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — definition of “interest” and its statutory scope (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=267.)

Code § 267 (both subdivisions (a) and (b), including the full fifteen-item list), fetched twice independently (two separate requests using distinct User-Agent strings against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) with identical results. Several terms this list uses — for example, “employee benefit plan” (defined at Prob. Code § 266) and “creator of the interest” (defined at Prob. FORMAL REQUIREMENTS FOR A VALID DISCLAIMER
California Probate Code § 278 sets out three formal requirements a disclaimer must meet: it must be in writing, it must be signed by the disclaimant, and it must identify the creator of the interest, describe the interest to be disclaimed, and state the disclaimer and its extent — meaning whether the disclaimant is disclaiming the whole interest or only part of it. Beyond signing and content, Prob. Code § 280(a) separately requires that the written disclaimer be filed — with the superior court in the county administering the decedent's estate (or, if there is no administration, any county where administration would be proper), with the trustee, personal representative, other fiduciary, or person responsible for distributing the interest, with any other person having custody, possession, or legal title to the interest, or with the creator of the interest itself. A disclaimer that affects real property or an obligation secured by real property may also be acknowledged and recorded like a grant of real property, under Prob. Code § 280(b), though that subdivision states that failing to record it does not, by itself, affect the validity of a transaction with respect to the property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The disclaimer shall be in writing, shall be signed by the disclaimant, and shall: (a) Identify the creator of the interest. (b) Describe the interest to be disclaimed. (c) State the disclaimer and the extent of the disclaimer."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 278, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — writing, signature, and content requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=278.)
  "(a) A disclaimer shall be filed with any of the following: (1) The superior court in the county in which the estate of the decedent is administered or, if there is no administration of the decedent’s estate, the superior court in any county in which administration of the estate of the decedent would be proper. (2) The trustee, personal representative, other fiduciary, or person responsible for distributing the interest to the beneficiary. (3) Any other person having custody or possession of or legal title to the interest. (4) The creator of the interest."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 280(a), California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — where a disclaimer must be filed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=280.)

This clause does not address the guardian/conservator/personal-representative court-petition process under §§ 276–277, which imposes additional content and notice requirements beyond § 278 when someone other than the beneficiary personally is disclaiming on the beneficiary's behalf.

TIMING: NO FIXED DEADLINE, A NINE-MONTH SAFE HARBOR, AND A SEPARATE FEDERAL RULE
California's own disclaimer statute does not set a single fixed deadline. Prob. Code § 279(a) instead requires only that a disclaimer be filed within a reasonable time after the person able to disclaim acquires knowledge of the interest — an open-ended standard. Subdivision (b) then creates a safe harbor for most of the interest categories this part covers (an interest created under a will, by intestate succession, by exercise or nonexercise of a testamentary power of appointment, by surviving the death of a Totten-trust or P.O.D. depositor, under a life insurance or annuity contract, by surviving the death of a joint tenant, under an employee benefit plan, under an individual retirement account, annuity, or bond, or under a transfer-on-death beneficiary designation): a disclaimer filed within nine months after the creator of the interest's death, or nine months after the interest becomes indefeasibly vested, whichever is later, is conclusively presumed to have been filed within a reasonable time. Subdivisions (c), (d), and (e) of the same section set parallel nine-month presumption windows, measured from different triggering events, for a living-trust interest, a presently exercisable power of appointment, an inter vivos gift, a future estate, and other interests not otherwise listed; and subdivision (f) makes clear that missing these nine-month windows does not automatically invalidate a disclaimer — it only shifts the burden onto the disclaimant to show the filing was still within a reasonable time. This state-law nine-month presumption should not be confused with the separate nine-month deadline federal tax law imposes for a disclaimer to qualify for certain federal estate- and gift-tax treatment (commonly discussed as a “qualified disclaimer” under federal law) — a federal statute this document does not independently verify or address. California's own statute connects to federal law in one specific way, at Prob. Code § 295: if a disclaimer or transfer is treated under federal law (Title 26 of the United States Code and its regulations) as though the disclaimed interest had never been transferred to the beneficiary, then that disclaimer or transfer is also effective as a disclaimer under this California statute, regardless of any other provision of this part.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A disclaimer to be effective shall be filed within a reasonable time after the person able to disclaim acquires knowledge of the interest."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 279(a), California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — the reasonable-time filing standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=279.)
  "(b) In the case of any of the following interests, a disclaimer is conclusively presumed to have been filed within a reasonable time if it is filed within nine months after the death of the creator of the interest or within nine months after the interest becomes indefeasibly vested, whichever occurs later:"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 279(b), California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — nine-month conclusive presumption of timeliness (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=279.)
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of this part, if as a result of a disclaimer or transfer the disclaimed or transferred interest is treated pursuant to the provisions of Title 26 of the United States Code, as now or hereafter amended, or any successor statute thereto, and the regulations promulgated thereunder, as never having been transferred to the beneficiary, then the disclaimer or transfer is effective as a disclaimer under this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 295, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — disclaimers effective under federal law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=295.)

LEGAL EFFECT OF A VALID DISCLAIMER
Once effective, a disclaimer under this part has two main statutory consequences. First, under Prob. Code § 281, it is irrevocable and binding upon the beneficiary and all persons claiming by, through, or under the beneficiary, including creditors of the beneficiary — a disclaimant cannot later change their mind about property connected to Pat Morgan or anyone else. Second, Prob. Code § 282(a) sets the default rule for where a disclaimed interest goes: unless the creator of the interest has provided for a specific disposition in the event of a disclaimer, the disclaimed interest passes as if the disclaimant had predeceased the creator of the interest (for a present interest) or as if the disclaimant had died before the interest's taker became finally ascertained and indefeasibly vested (for a future interest), and the disclaimer relates back to the date of the creator's death or the determinative event for all purposes. Because the statute directs the property to descend under this predecease fiction — or under whatever alternative disposition the creator of the interest itself specified — rather than to wherever the disclaimant might prefer, this section does not give a disclaimant the power to redirect a disclaimed interest to a person of the disclaimant's own choosing. Subdivision (b) adds two further, narrower qualifications for a disclaimer filed on or after January 1, 1985: the disclaiming beneficiary is not treated as having predeceased the decedent for purposes of determining which generation an estate divides at under Part 6 (commencing with Section 240) or under a will, trust, or other instrument's own generation-based provisions, and is likewise not treated as having predeceased the decedent when applying Prob. Code § 6409(d) or § 6410(b).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A disclaimer, when effective, is irrevocable and binding upon the beneficiary and all persons claiming by, through, or under the beneficiary, including creditors of the beneficiary."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 281, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — irrevocability of an effective disclaimer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=281.)
  "(a) Unless the creator of the interest provides for a specific disposition of the interest in the event of a disclaimer, the interest disclaimed shall descend, go, be distributed, or continue to be held (1) as to a present interest, as if the disclaimant had predeceased the creator of the interest or (2) as to a future interest, as if the disclaimant had died before the event determining that the taker of the interest had become finally ascertained and the taker’s interest indefeasibly vested. A disclaimer relates back for all purposes to the date of the death of the creator of the disclaimed interest or the determinative event, as the case may be. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), where the disclaimer is filed on or after January 1, 1985: (1) The beneficiary is not treated as having predeceased the decedent for the purpose of determining the generation at which the division of the estate is to be made under Part 6 (commencing with Section 240) or other provision of a will, trust, or other instrument. (2) The beneficiary of a disclaimed interest is not treated as having predeceased the decedent for the purpose of applying subdivision (d) of Section 6409 or subdivision (b) of Section 6410."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 282, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — the predecease mechanism governing where a disclaimed interest passes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=282.)

PARTIAL DISCLAIMERS AND BARS TO DISCLAIMING
Section 275 — already quoted in this document's disclaimer_who_may_disclaim clause — states the partial-disclaimer rule in the same sentence as the core right: a beneficiary may disclaim any interest in whole or in part. A disclaimant is not required to give up an entire interest in order to disclaim at all. Prob. Code § 285 then sets the principal bar: subdivision (a) states that a disclaimer may not be made after the beneficiary has accepted the interest sought to be disclaimed, and subdivision (b) defines what counts as acceptance — a voluntary assignment, conveyance, encumbrance, pledge, or transfer of the interest, or a contract to do so; executing a written waiver of the right to disclaim under § 284; accepting the interest or a benefit under it; or having the interest sold at a judicial sale — while carving out an exception for a beneficiary who makes a gratuitous conveyance of their entire interest to whoever would have received it under an otherwise qualified disclaimer. Subdivision (c) further allows a beneficiary who already accepted one interest to still disclaim a second, later interest that came to the beneficiary only because someone else disclaimed first, so long as the beneficiary had no knowledge of that second interest at the time of the original acceptance; and subdivision (d) clarifies that a joint tenant's acceptance of the original joint-tenancy interest is not, by itself, an acceptance of the separate interest the joint tenant later receives by surviving another joint tenant. Separately, Prob. Code § 286 states that the right to disclaim exists regardless of any limitation imposed on the interest of a beneficiary in the nature of an expressed or implied spendthrift provision or similar restriction — a spendthrift clause in a trust does not, by itself, block a beneficiary from disclaiming.

  "A beneficiary may disclaim any interest, in whole or in part, by filing a disclaimer as provided in this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 275, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — the right to disclaim in whole or in part (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=275.)
  "(a) A disclaimer may not be made after the beneficiary has accepted the interest sought to be disclaimed. (b) For the purpose of this section, a beneficiary has accepted an interest if any of the following occurs before a disclaimer is filed with respect to that interest: (1) The beneficiary, or someone acting on behalf of the beneficiary, makes a voluntary assignment, conveyance, encumbrance, pledge, or transfer of the interest or part thereof, or contracts to do so; provided, however, that a beneficiary will not have accepted an interest if the beneficiary makes a gratuitous conveyance or transfer of the beneficiary’s entire interest in property to the person or persons who would have received the property had the beneficiary made an otherwise qualified disclaimer pursuant to this part. (2) The beneficiary, or someone acting on behalf of the beneficiary, executes a written waiver under Section 284 of the right to disclaim the interest. (3) The beneficiary, or someone acting on behalf of the beneficiary, accepts the interest or part thereof or benefit thereunder. (4) The interest or part thereof is sold at a judicial sale. (c) An acceptance does not preclude a beneficiary from thereafter disclaiming all or part of an interest if both of the following requirements are met: (1) The beneficiary became entitled to the interest because another person disclaimed an interest. (2) The beneficiary or other person acting on behalf of the beneficiary at the time of the acceptance had no knowledge of the interest to which the beneficiary so became entitled. (d) The acceptance by a joint tenant of the joint tenancy interest created when the joint tenancy is created is not an acceptance by the joint tenant of the interest created when the joint tenant survives the death of another joint tenant."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 285, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — bar to disclaiming after acceptance of the interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=285.)

  — Cal. Prob. Code § 286, California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — spendthrift provisions do not bar the right to disclaim (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=286.)

DISCLAIMER OF INTEREST DECLARATION
I, Jordan Alex Lee, am a beneficiary entitled, but for this disclaimer, to the following interest: My one-third interest in the residence at 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105, which was created by Pat Morgan as the creator of the interest within the meaning of California Probate Code § 263. I have not accepted this interest, or any benefit under it, before signing this disclaimer. I hereby decline, refuse, renounce, and disclaim that interest, in whole or to the extent described above, under California Probate Code Division 2, Part 8 (commencing with Section 260). I have not directed, and this disclaimer does not direct, that the disclaimed interest be given to any particular person; under California Probate Code § 282, the disclaimed interest will instead pass as provided by the instrument that created it or, if that instrument does not provide otherwise, as if I had predeceased Pat Morgan.

SIGNATURE AND NOTARIZATION
I declare that the foregoing is true and correct to the best of my knowledge. Executed on September 2, 2026, at San Francisco, California.

☐ _________________________ Jordan Alex Lee, Disclaimant   Date: September 2, 2026

If this disclaimer affects real property or an obligation secured by real property, California Probate Code § 280(b) allows it to be acknowledged before a notary public and recorded in the same manner as a grant of real property; the acknowledgment below is included for that purpose and is not required for a disclaimer that does not affect real property.

State of California
County of _________________________

On September 2, 2026, before me, _________________________, a Notary Public, personally appeared Jordan Alex Lee, who proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the person whose name is subscribed to the within instrument, and acknowledged that they executed the same in their authorized capacity, and that by their signature on the instrument the person executed the instrument.

I certify under PENALTY OF PERJURY under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing paragraph is true and correct.

WITNESS my hand and official seal.

Signature of Notary Public: _________________________ (Seal)

expectedJSON.body: California's own disclaimer statute does not set a single fixed deadline. Prob. Code § 279(a) instead requires only that a disclaimer be filed within a reasonable time after the person able to disclaim acquires knowledge of the interest — an open-ended standard. Subdivision (b) then creates a safe harbor for most of the interest categories this part covers (an interest created under a will, by intestate succession, by exercise or nonexercise of a testamentary power of appointment, by surviving the death of a Totten-trust or P.O.D. depositor, under a life insurance or annuity contract, by surviving the death of a joint tenant, under an employee benefit plan, under an individual retirement account, annuity, or bond, or under a transfer-on-death beneficiary designation): a disclaimer filed within nine months after the creator of the interest's death, or nine months after the interest becomes indefeasibly vested, whichever is later, is conclusively presumed to have been filed within a reasonable time. Subdivisions (c), (d), and (e) of the same section set parallel nine-month presumption windows, measured from different triggering events, for a living-trust interest, a presently exercisable power of appointment, an inter vivos gift, a future estate, and other interests not otherwise listed; and subdivision (f) makes clear that missing these nine-month windows does not automatically invalidate a disclaimer — it only shifts the burden onto the disclaimant to show the filing was still within a reasonable time. This state-law nine-month presumption should not be confused with the separate nine-month deadline federal tax law imposes for a disclaimer to qualify for certain federal estate- and gift-tax treatment (commonly discussed as a “qualified disclaimer” under federal law) — a federal statute this document does not independently verify or address. California's own statute connects to federal law in one specific way, at Prob. Code § 295: if a disclaimer or transfer is treated under federal law (Title 26 of the United States Code and its regulations) as though the disclaimed interest had never been transferred to the beneficiary, then that disclaimer or transfer is also effective as a disclaimer under this California statute, regardless of any other provision of this part.

expectedJSON.body: Once effective, a disclaimer under this part has two main statutory consequences. First, under Prob. Code § 281, it is irrevocable and binding upon the beneficiary and all persons claiming by, through, or under the beneficiary, including creditors of the beneficiary — a disclaimant cannot later change their mind about property connected to Pat Morgan or anyone else. Second, Prob. Code § 282(a) sets the default rule for where a disclaimed interest goes: unless the creator of the interest has provided for a specific disposition in the event of a disclaimer, the disclaimed interest passes as if the disclaimant had predeceased the creator of the interest (for a present interest) or as if the disclaimant had died before the interest's taker became finally ascertained and indefeasibly vested (for a future interest), and the disclaimer relates back to the date of the creator's death or the determinative event for all purposes. Because the statute directs the property to descend under this predecease fiction — or under whatever alternative disposition the creator of the interest itself specified — rather than to wherever the disclaimant might prefer, this section does not give a disclaimant the power to redirect a disclaimed interest to a person of the disclaimant's own choosing. Subdivision (b) adds two further, narrower qualifications for a disclaimer filed on or after January 1, 1985: the disclaiming beneficiary is not treated as having predeceased the decedent for purposes of determining which generation an estate divides at under Part 6 (commencing with Section 240) or under a will, trust, or other instrument's own generation-based provisions, and is likewise not treated as having predeceased the decedent when applying Prob. Code § 6409(d) or § 6410(b).

citations.quote: (a) Unless the creator of the interest provides for a specific disposition of the interest in the event of a disclaimer, the interest disclaimed shall descend, go, be distributed, or continue to be held (1) as to a present interest, as if the disclaimant had predeceased the creator of the interest or (2) as to a future interest, as if the disclaimant had died before the event determining that the taker of the interest had become finally ascertained and the taker’s interest indefeasibly vested. A disclaimer relates back for all purposes to the date of the death of the creator of the disclaimed interest or the determinative event, as the case may be. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), where the disclaimer is filed on or after January 1, 1985: (1) The beneficiary is not treated as having predeceased the decedent for the purpose of determining the generation at which the division of the estate is to be made under Part 6 (commencing with Section 240) or other provision of a will, trust, or other instrument. (2) The beneficiary of a disclaimed interest is not treated as having predeceased the decedent for the purpose of applying subdivision (d) of Section 6409 or subdivision (b) of Section 6410.

expectedJSON.body: Section 275 — already quoted in this document's disclaimer_who_may_disclaim clause — states the partial-disclaimer rule in the same sentence as the core right: a beneficiary may disclaim any interest in whole or in part. A disclaimant is not required to give up an entire interest in order to disclaim at all. Prob. Code § 285 then sets the principal bar: subdivision (a) states that a disclaimer may not be made after the beneficiary has accepted the interest sought to be disclaimed, and subdivision (b) defines what counts as acceptance — a voluntary assignment, conveyance, encumbrance, pledge, or transfer of the interest, or a contract to do so; executing a written waiver of the right to disclaim under § 284; accepting the interest or a benefit under it; or having the interest sold at a judicial sale — while carving out an exception for a beneficiary who makes a gratuitous conveyance of their entire interest to whoever would have received it under an otherwise qualified disclaimer. Subdivision (c) further allows a beneficiary who already accepted one interest to still disclaim a second, later interest that came to the beneficiary only because someone else disclaimed first, so long as the beneficiary had no knowledge of that second interest at the time of the original acceptance; and subdivision (d) clarifies that a joint tenant's acceptance of the original joint-tenancy interest is not, by itself, an acceptance of the separate interest the joint tenant later receives by surviving another joint tenant. Separately, Prob. Code § 286 states that the right to disclaim exists regardless of any limitation imposed on the interest of a beneficiary in the nature of an expressed or implied spendthrift provision or similar restriction — a spendthrift clause in a trust does not, by itself, block a beneficiary from disclaiming.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — bar to disclaiming after acceptance of the interest
citations.quote: (a) A disclaimer may not be made after the beneficiary has accepted the interest sought to be disclaimed. (b) For the purpose of this section, a beneficiary has accepted an interest if any of the following occurs before a disclaimer is filed with respect to that interest: (1) The beneficiary, or someone acting on behalf of the beneficiary, makes a voluntary assignment, conveyance, encumbrance, pledge, or transfer of the interest or part thereof, or contracts to do so; provided, however, that a beneficiary will not have accepted an interest if the beneficiary makes a gratuitous conveyance or transfer of the beneficiary’s entire interest in property to the person or persons who would have received the property had the beneficiary made an otherwise qualified disclaimer pursuant to this part. (2) The beneficiary, or someone acting on behalf of the beneficiary, executes a written waiver under Section 284 of the right to disclaim the interest. (3) The beneficiary, or someone acting on behalf of the beneficiary, accepts the interest or part thereof or benefit thereunder. (4) The interest or part thereof is sold at a judicial sale. (c) An acceptance does not preclude a beneficiary from thereafter disclaiming all or part of an interest if both of the following requirements are met: (1) The beneficiary became entitled to the interest because another person disclaimed an interest. (2) The beneficiary or other person acting on behalf of the beneficiary at the time of the acceptance had no knowledge of the interest to which the beneficiary so became entitled. (d) The acceptance by a joint tenant of the joint tenancy interest created when the joint tenancy is created is not an acceptance by the joint tenant of the interest created when the joint tenant survives the death of another joint tenant.
